svg.title: How MagicFocus Works
svg.desc: How MagicFocus works, drawn from the left of the rig: a Canon EOS R5 C in a Kondor Blue cage with an RF 24-70mm f/2.8L lens. A seamless gear ring sits on the lens focus ring. A 15 mm carbon rod runs forward from the cage front rod clamp beside the top of the lens, and a Tilta Nucleus Nano II motor hangs from it, thumbscrew up, its gear on the gear ring. A second rod just above, clamped to the cage, carries a TFmini-S lidar at the front; just behind it the MagicFocus stack, a CoreS3, a Gateway H2 module and a DIN Base, screen up, its DIN Base sitting on a rod clamp; and at the back a SmallRig NP-F battery plate with an NP-F battery on it, which powers the motor through a USB-C cable along the rod into the motor's USB-C socket 1. The lidar cable runs to Port B on the front of the stack. 1, measure: the lidar times infrared light to a person walking towards the camera, about 100 times a second, giving the distance d. 2, convert: MagicFocus filters the distance and looks it up in the lens calibration to get a motor position. 3, send: the Gateway H2 radios the position to the motor. 4, turn: the motor gear turns the gear ring, and the focus ring with it. 5, focus: the lens focuses on the person at distance d. The calibration is made once per lens by focusing by eye at two or three distances. The system is open loop: nothing measures where focus ends up, so accuracy depends on the calibration, a lens that turns ring movement into the same focus every time, and the lidar spot landing on the subject.
svg.text: The lidar measures the distance, MagicFocus turns it into a motor position, and the motor turns the lens's focus ring.

text.tspan: You focus by eye at two or three distances and press Save to SD; step 2 interpolates between those points.
Nothing measures where focus ends up, and the motor only acknowledges packets. Accuracy depends on the calibration,

g.text: on a lens that turns ring movement into the same focus every time, and on the lidar spot landing on the subject.
The lidar measures from where it sits, not from the sensor; the calibration absorbs that offset.
